units.title: Brain Drain
units.intro: Grammar: the subject–verb–complement (SVC) pattern and clauses: noun phrases, noun clauses, adjective (relative) clauses and adjectival complements.

cards.title: SVC sentences and adjectival complements
rule: **SVC:** Subject + linking verb (*be, become, seem, look, feel*) + Complement (a noun or adjective that describes the subject): *Many graduates **became** doctors.* *The problem **seems** serious.*
An **adjectival complement** follows an adjective: *I am **happy to help**.* *She is **sure that she will return**.*

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Since the local library was renovated last year, the number of visitors ________ significantly.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The subject is 'the number of visitors' (singular).
The sentence describes an action that started in the past (renovated last year) and continues to have relevance in the present, requiring the present perfect tense (has/have + V3).
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often see 'visitors' (plural) and choose 'have increased'.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The science teacher asked Dawit, 'Why ________ your assignment on time yesterday?'

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** This is a direct question in the past simple tense.
Questions require subject-auxiliary inversion: Wh-word + auxiliary (didn't) + Subject (you) + base verb (complete).
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Option A incorrectly combines 'didn't' with the past tense verb 'completed'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The rare African manuscript ________ from the national archives before the guards noticed the broken window.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The sentence describes two past events: the manuscript being stolen and the guards noticing the broken window. The theft happened before the guards noticed it, requiring the past perfect passive voice (had been + V3).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Option A ('was stolen') is simple past passive. While grammatically correct in isolation, it does not correctly sequence the two past actions. Option D ('has been stolen') is present perfect, which cannot be paired with the simple past past clause ('before the guards noticed').

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
እዚ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ክልተ ኣብ ሕሉፍ ግዜ ዝተፈጸሙ ድርጊታት የነጻጽር። እቲ ጽሑፍ ዝተሰረቐሉ ግዜ፡ እቶም ሓለውቲ ቅድሚ ምርኣዮም ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ካብቲ ሓደ ሕሉፍ ግዜ ንላዕሊ ዝቐደመ (earlier past) እዩ። ስለዚ ሕሉፍ ፍጹም ጥንሳዊ መዋቕር (past perfect passive) 'had been stolen' (Option B) ክንጥቀም ኣለና።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Each of the candidates who applied for the engineering position ________ a written test.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The subject of the sentence is 'Each' (singular), which always takes a singular verb and auxiliary (Each → singular verb).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often look at the plural noun closest to the verb ('candidates') and incorrectly select the plural auxiliary 'have' (Option B) or 'are' (Option C). This is a classic subject-verb agreement trap.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'Each' (ነፍሲ ወከፍ) ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ብሰዋስው ወግዒ ነጸላ (singular) እዩ። ስለዚ ምስኡ ዝኸይድ ነጸላ ግሲ 'has to take' (Option A) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። 'candidates' (ሕጹያት) ዝብል ቃል ብዙሕ ስለ ዝኾነ 'have' ምምራጽ ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In "The children are happy", what is "happy"?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "are" is a linking verb.

**Step 2:** "happy" describes the subject "The children".

**Step 3:** This is S-V-C, so "happy" is an adjective complement.

**Tip:** An adjective (relative) clause describes a noun: who for people, which for things, whose for possession, where for places. Non-defining clauses take commas.

cards.title: Adjective (relative) clauses
rule: An **adjective clause** describes a noun and begins with **who** (people), **which** (things), **that** (people or things), **whose** (possession), **where** (places), **when** (time): *Doctors **who leave the country** are hard to replace.*
**Defining** clauses tell us which one (no commas). **Non-defining** clauses add extra information (with commas; never *that*): *Asmara, **which is the capital**, is clean.*

examples.text: The engineer who designed the dam is Eritrean.
The book what I read was good.
examples.fix: The book that/which I read was good.

examples.text: My uncle, who lives abroad, sends money.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The book what I read was good."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** An **adjective clause** describes a noun and begins with **who** (people), **which** (things), **that** (people or things), **whose** (possession), **where** (places), **when** (time): *Doctors **who leave the country** are hard to replace.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The book what I read was good." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The book that/which I read was good."
**Check:** **Defining** clauses tell us which one (no commas). **Non-defining** clauses add extra information (with commas; never *that*): *Asmara, **which is the capital**, is clean.*

cards.answer: The book that/which I read was good.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **WHO** for people, **WHICH** for things, **WHERE** for places, **WHOSE** for owners.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: SVC sentences use a linking verb plus a complement (noun or adjective). Adjective clauses (who, which, that, whose, where, when) describe nouns; non-defining ones have commas and never use that. Adjectival complements complete adjectives (eager to, sure that).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: My car, _____ was expensive, was stolen two days ago.
cards.why: This is a non-defining relative clause (set off by commas). For things, we use 'which' in non-defining clauses. 'That' cannot be used after a comma in this context.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The village ____ my grandparents live has no electricity.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The clause describes a place and means "in which".

**Step 2:** Use "where" for places.

**Step 3:** "which" would need "in which".

**Tip:** An adjective (relative) clause describes a noun: who for people, which for things, whose for possession, where for places. Non-defining clauses take commas.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The students ____ finished early went home.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The clause describes people (the students).

**Step 2:** They are the subject of "finished".

**Step 3:** Use "who".

**Tip:** An adjective (relative) clause describes a noun: who for people, which for things, whose for possession, where for places. Non-defining clauses take commas.

glossary.meaning: A verb like be, seem, become that links the subject to a complement.
who, which, that, whose: starts an adjective clause.

tips.text: **WHO** for people, **WHICH** for things, **WHERE** for places, **WHOSE** for owners.
